Yes. 

The story makes sophisticated use of metaphor and figurative language to convey the themes of aging, grief, and estrangement without stating them explicitly. 

First, the ferry and its sputtering motor serve as a central extended metaphor for Ilse's life and resilience after her husband's death. When Jonas remarks at the beginning that the motor sounds like it is about to fall apart, Ilse insists, "It runs." At the end of the story, she offers to take him right back across the river "so you see that nothing is falling apart." She is no longer just talking about the boat, but reassuring her son—and perhaps herself—that she is holding her life together on her own. Similarly, her reflection that "the river didn't carry you to the other bank on its own when you got old" operates both literally (regarding the physical strength needed to pull the cable ferry) and metaphorically (regarding the passage of time and the effort required to keep going after a loss).

Additionally, the story uses brief, evocative similes and idioms that lend authenticity to the characters. Ilse's internal comparisons—viewing Jonas's wheeled suitcase as being pulled "like a dog" and noting that infrequent visitors take in the scenery "like an appraisal" (*wie ein Gutachten*)—efficiently highlight the cultural and emotional distance between the rural, practical mother and her urbanized, estranged son. Finally, Jonas's use of the common German idiom *"Ich bin nicht aus Zucker"* ("I'm not made of sugar") feels natural in the dialogue, showing his desire to prove to his mother that he hasn't gone soft.
